items.content:
Two posts today. The one about an 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability got far more attention than the one about CAIRN/ARTEX.

I think the second topic is far more important.

I’ve been following vulnerabilities long enough to recognize the pattern. They’re discovered, exploited, patched, and replaced by the next ones. AI will accelerate this process dramatically, but the fundamental cycle remains the same.

What we’re seeing with AI-driven attack frameworks is something different. They’re starting to change how attacks are conducted in general, not just how vulnerabilities are discovered or exploited.

They allow attackers to plan, adapt, make decisions, and scale entire operations with far less human effort. And vulnerability exploitation is just a small part of what these systems can do.

I think this will have a much more profound and lasting impact on cybersecurity than the current wave of AI-discovered vulnerabilities.

Yet the individual CVE gets all the attention.

Meta's second-generation network card driver also lands upstream, so Meta keeps shipping drivers for its own data centre hardware straight into mainline.
